venue: The Art Station (The Gallery at Big Shanty), Kennesaw
blurb:
Saturday is your last chance to see Southern Superstition at The Gallery at The Art Station in Kennesaw. The closing reception runs from 2 to 4pm, which makes it an easy stop to pair with anything else you've got going on in the area that day.

If you haven't been through the exhibition yet, this is the window. Local art receptions are a good reminder that interesting things are happening right in the neighborhood, and The Art Station consistently puts together thoughtful shows. Free to attend, no pressure, just come see it before it closes.
scoring_notes: The 'last chance' closing reception angle gives this genuine urgency that a mid-run gallery event wouldn't have. Free admission fits a casual weekend slot well. Kennesaw location is close to East Cobb. Scores lower on demographic fit and audience match because art receptions are a narrower interest draw, but the closing-night dynamic and free admission make it worth including as a lighter listing.

event_name: Book Signing & Authors Talk: "35 Natural Wonders of Georgia to See Before You Die"
venue: Art Sandy Springs / Abernathy Art Center, Sandy Springs
blurb:
If you've lived in Georgia long enough to feel like you've seen most of it, this Saturday's author talk might prove you wrong. Environment Sandy Springs is hosting a presentation and book signing for "35 Natural Wonders of Georgia to See Before You Die," a bucket-list guide to the state's most spectacular outdoor spots.

It's free to attend, runs from 3:30 to 6pm at the Abernathy Art Center in Sandy Springs, and it's a genuinely low-key way to spend a Saturday afternoon. If you've got teens who are starting to think about road trips, or you're looking for next year's camping and hiking list, you'll probably leave with a few ideas circled.
scoring_notes: Free event with a practical takeaway (a bucket list guide) is a solid fit for the educated, outdoorsy segment of the East Cobb audience. Sandy Springs location is close enough to be reasonable. The family and teen angle adds relevance for the established-family segment. Uniqueness is moderate, but the specific author presentation format and free admission make it more than a passive event.

venue: Bailey Performance Center, Kennesaw State University
blurb:
The Georgia Youth Symphony Orchestra is one of the best youth orchestra programs in the Southeast, and this Sunday they take the stage at KSU's Bailey Performance Center for their November concert. The lineup includes the Honors String Quartet, Flute Choir, String Symposium, and Philharmonic, so there's real range across the evening.

If you have a kid who plays an instrument, or a kid who used to, or you just appreciate watching young musicians perform at a genuinely high level, this is a great Sunday night. The Bailey is a beautiful hall and it's right in your backyard. Worth the trip.
scoring_notes: Strong fit for the East Cobb family demographic, particularly households with teen or college-age kids who may have grown up in music programs. Empty nesters who supported kids through music will also connect. KSU location is close and familiar. Uniqueness is moderate since GYSO concerts happen throughout the year, but the specific date and multi-ensemble lineup make this particular concert worth featuring.

event_name: Lumiere Lounge Jazz Talk with Trey Wright
venue: The Earl and Rachel Smith Strand Theatre, Marietta
blurb:
If you've ever wanted to actually understand jazz, not just nod along to it, this is your Thursday night. KSU Professor Trey Wright is bringing his Jazz Talk series to the Strand's intimate Lumiere Lounge, and this session focuses on Charlie Christian, the guitarist who essentially changed how jazz worked.

Thirty seats. One drink ticket included with admission. Doors at 7, presentation at 7:30. It's small on purpose, which means you're getting a real conversation, not a lecture hall experience. Must be 21 or older.

The Strand doesn't do this every night. If you're even a little curious about the history of jazz guitar, this is a sharp way to spend a Thursday.
scoring_notes: Highly limited (30 seats) makes it genuinely exclusive and worth flagging. Interactive jazz education format is a strong fit for the educated, culturally curious East Cobb audience. Adult-only 21+ skew works well for the empty nester segment. The drink-included detail and intimate venue give it a premium feel that matches the $118K median income audience. Niche interest lowers the demographic fit slightly, but those who are interested will really want to know about it.

blurb:
Thirty-plus local restaurants, live music on the Main Street stage, a beer garden with the game on, a kids zone with inflatables, and holiday shopping from local Georgia Grown vendors. That's the full picture for Taste of Kennesaw this Saturday in downtown Kennesaw, and it runs all day from 11am to 6pm.

This is a genuinely good excuse to get outside before the weather really turns. It's also the kind of event that works whether you show up solo, bring the whole family, or make it a thing with neighbors. Sample your way through the lineup, grab a beer, and do some early holiday shopping while you're at it. No tickets, no cover, just show up.
scoring_notes: Annual food festival with 30+ restaurants is a strong community draw. The mix of beer garden, live music, kids zone, and holiday shopping hits multiple East Cobb household types (established families and empty nesters alike). Free admission is genuinely appealing at any income level for a casual Saturday outing. Uniqueness score is lower because it's a recurring annual event, but the specific date and full-day format give it enough event-ness to include.

event_name: The Last Days of Judas Iscariot
blurb:
This is not a Sunday school play. The Last Days of Judas Iscariot drops one of history's most infamous figures into a surreal courtroom trial, where witnesses include Mother Teresa, Sigmund Freud, and Satan himself. Written by Pulitzer Prize-winning playwright Stephen Adly Guirgis, it's equal parts hilarious and gut-punching, the kind of theater that sticks with you after you drive home.

The production runs multiple nights this week at Stillwell Theater in Kennesaw, with performances on Thursday, Friday, Saturday, and Sunday. Director Jacqueline Springfield is steering a show that wrestles with guilt, forgiveness, free will, and what mercy actually looks like when you push on it hard enough.

Fair warning: mature content throughout. But if you're up for theater that actually challenges you to think, this one earns it. Grab tickets before the run closes.
scoring_notes: Pulitzer Prize-winning playwright gives this real cultural credibility. Multi-night run during the issue window makes it timely. Skews adult, which works well for both the empty nester segment and couples looking for a real night out. The provocative, philosophical angle is a strong fit for the educated East Cobb audience (65%+ college educated). Mature content note is relevant and should be included.

blurb:
A century ago on Halloween night, Harry Houdini died. And somehow, his name still stops people cold. Magician, escape artist, aviator, cultural icon, there will never be another one like him.

This Saturday at the William Root House in Marietta, James Freeman of Freeman and Fugate Oddities Company is presenting an up-close look at the man behind the myth. The evening is part lecture, part mini-museum, with rare artifacts that were personally owned by Houdini himself. You're not watching a documentary. You're in the same room as the actual objects.

Space is limited, and this is a one-night event. If you've ever been even a little curious about Houdini, this is the excuse you've been waiting for.
scoring_notes: One-night-only lecture tied to a genuine cultural moment (the centennial of Houdini's death on Halloween 1926). The rare-artifact angle makes it genuinely unique, not just another talk. Skews adult, which fits both the established family and empty nester segments. Marietta location is close and accessible for East Cobb residents. Limited space adds real urgency.
